strengths: The paper tackles an important and well-motivated question: how much repository-level editing capability can be internalized into model weights via training data, disentangling this from inference-time scaffolding complexity.

The data construction pipeline is rigorous and well-documented: bot filtering, core-language rules, issue linking, and a genuinely verifiable round-trip Search/Replace reconstruction (Algorithm 1) that guarantees bit-wise exact reconstruction, which is a meaningful improvement over noisy diff-based corpora.
Scale and diversity of the released corpus (2M verified PRs, 12 languages, 45K+ repos) substantially exceeds prior natural code-change corpora in structured, multi-file, verified form (Table 1).

Strong and consistent empirical gains over a carefully constructed, well-matched StarCoder2-style baseline (same token budget, same base model) isolate the contribution of data quality/format rather than just scale, and ablations (Table 8, Table 9) further decompose the sources of improvement (S/R format, issue linking, error-driven augmentation).

Non-trivial decontamination effort, including repo-level exclusion, SHA-256/n-gram matching, and an embedding-based semantic leakage analysis (Appendix A.7) showing no positive correlation between train-test similarity and resolve rate, which is more rigorous than typical practice.

Broad generalization studies (7B scale, multilingual Multi-SWE-bench, and OpenHands agentic transfer) show the learned capability is not narrowly overfit to the specific Agentless scaffold or model size used for the main results.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility documentation in the appendix (prompts, hyperparameters, filtering rules, dataset schema).
weaknesses: All experiments use a single base model family (Qwen2.5-Coder, 32B and 7B); it is unclear whether the Clean-PR recipe transfers to other architectures/tokenizers, and the paper explicitly defers this to future work.

No variance/error bars or multiple-run statistics are reported for Pass@1 numbers on SWE-bench Lite/Verified, which are known to be sensitive to patch-application and grading nuances; single-run point estimates make it hard to assess the reliability of gains, especially smaller deltas in ablations.

External comparisons (Table 7) against SWE-Gym, Lingma-SWE, and SWE-Fixer are not fully controlled — these systems differ in training data, scaffolding, and possibly evaluation protocol/settings, so claims of 'surpassing 72B baselines' should be interpreted cautiously rather than as a controlled comparison.

The dataset is only 'planned' for release at submission time; given the paper's central claim rests on data quality/scale, reviewers cannot verify pipeline outputs or dataset statistics independently before release.

Filtering heuristics (bot regex patterns, keyword blocklists for titles/descriptions, core-file extension rules) are entirely heuristic; no human-annotated precision/recall validation of the noise-filtering pipeline is reported, so the true quality of the 'Clean' 18.59% subset is asserted rather than directly measured.

The Search/Replace edit format itself is adopted from prior work (Agentless/Xia et al.), so the core methodological novelty lies primarily in the data pipeline and training recipe rather than in a new modeling or algorithmic contribution.

Some explanatory claims (e.g., why multilingual training improves single-language SWE-bench performance) are speculative and not substantiated by deeper mechanistic analysis beyond aggregate score differences.

strengths: Constructs the largest publicly-releasable PR-derived corpus (2M verified instances, 12 languages) via a rigorous, well-documented pipeline (bot/noise filtering, issue linking, Search/Replace reconstruction with round-trip byte-wise verification), addressing a genuine gap between noisy commit-level corpora and expensive SWE-bench-style datasets.

Extensive and carefully controlled ablations isolate the individual contributions of the pipeline: edit format (S/R vs. diff), issue-augmented context, error-driven augmentation, and multi-language vs. Python-only training, each showing consistent, interpretable gains.

Strong empirical results across multiple axes of generalization: 32B main results, 7B scale transfer, multilingual evaluation (Multi-SWE-bench Flash), and transfer into a different inference paradigm (OpenHands agentic loop), suggesting the learned capability is not merely overfit to the Agentless scaffold.

Thoughtful decontamination protocol (repo-level exclusion, SHA-256 exact matching, n-gram/Jaccard filtering, plus a semantic similarity/leakage correlation analysis) that goes beyond typical practice and helps substantiate that gains reflect generalization rather than leakage.

High reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with the verification algorithm, exact prompts for all three Agentless stages, hyperparameters, dataset schema, and a stated intent to release the dataset.

Efficiency story is compelling: the 32B model with simplified Agentless scaffolding outperforms larger 72B agentic baselines and a same-size OpenHands-trained baseline (SWE-Gym), supporting the central claim that data quality can substitute for scaffold complexity.
weaknesses: The primary baseline ('StarCoder2-style') is self-implemented by the authors rather than an existing published system, so the comparison, while described as faithful, could still embed implementation choices that indirectly favor Clean-PR; an independent or more standardized baseline would strengthen the claim.

Evaluation is confined to a single base model family (Qwen2.5-Coder); generalization to other pretrained backbones or tokenizers is explicitly left to future work, limiting confidence that the recipe is architecture-agnostic.

SWE-bench Lite/Verified are relatively small (300/500 instances) and results appear to be single runs without variance/seed reporting, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of reported gains (e.g., the ~2-3 point differences in some ablations).

The large Pass@1 vs. Pass@10 gap (Figure 3) indicates the likelihood-based decoding/ranking is a bottleneck the paper identifies but does not address, leaving the practical upper bound of the approach unexplored.

Comparisons to external 72B baselines (Table 7) rely on numbers copied from original papers under potentially different evaluation protocols/scaffolds, so the 'half the parameters, better performance' claim should be interpreted cautiously.

Issue-linking relies on simple regex heuristics over PR/issue text with no reported precision/recall for correct issue-PR association, leaving some uncertainty about how much noise remains in the 'issue-augmented intent' signal.
The dataset release is only 'planned,' so full reproducibility (beyond the algorithmic description) cannot yet be independently verified by reviewers or the community.
